scenes.narration: Every minute, more than {claim:cited.market.youtube_500h_per_min} of new video go up on YouTube. Most of it only works if you can see and hear it.
{claim:cited.gbd.blind_2020} people are blind. They need to hear what is on screen.
Erika Wolf, writing for the American Council of the Blind, remembers leaving shows not having any inkling of what really took place.
{claim:cited.who.hearing_430m} live with disabling hearing loss. They need captions that also say what sounds.
{claim:cited.oecd.piaac_lit_level1_oecd_avg} of adults read at the lowest levels. They need simpler words. And many people need their own language.

Doing this by hand takes about {claim:cited.market.maa_20_hours} for one hour of TV, at {claim:cited.price.3play_industry_range_low} to {claim:cited.price.3play_industry_range_high} a minute. So most video never gets it.
Let's see a real NASA talk about the Hubble telescope. First, close your eyes, and listen like a blind viewer.
He said: this is Hubble's famous photograph. But if you can't see the screen, you never find out what it shows.
No pause in his speech, so AccessCast held the picture while the description played. Gemma 4 on AMD wrote it, and code checked it.
This is AccessCast. One video for every viewer: people who can't see, can't hear, or need simpler words, and people who speak Hindi, Italian, Spanish, French or Portuguese.
On our site, every viewer picks what they need, and the same video plays for them.
If you can't see the screen, a voice describes what happens, in the pauses.
If you can't hear, captions show what is said, and the sounds.
If reading is hard, the same lines, in simpler words.
And in Hindi, Italian, Spanish, French and Portuguese, each with its own voice. Listen.
How does it work? Whisper listens. Gemma 4 31B, on AMD, looks and writes. Code checks every line, Gemma repairs what fails, and a person approves.
On that NASA clip, Gemma looks at frames from each scene, and lists only what it can see.
From that list alone, it writes one line inside a word budget: a man in a NASA polo shirt speaks to the camera.
Code stops it: a blind viewer already hears him speak, so it wastes the pause. The model never judges its own line.
It goes back to Gemma with the rule it broke. The new line, he looks at the camera, passes.
Every line keeps its record for the reviewer: the frames, the checks and every repair.
The rule at the heart of AccessCast: the model proposes, code decides. Only an answer that passes every check reaches a viewer.
We attack it on purpose: simplify, press the button three times within ten seconds. Anyone can run this live.

An answer that drops the ten seconds is blocked. In our recorded test, Gemma dropped it in {claim:e11.A5_number.production.gemma_failed} of {claim:e11.A5_number.production.tries} tries, and our checks blocked every one.
Or type your own caption. Our number check stopped an Italian line that turned 5 pm into 17:00, and the repair passed.

scenes.narration: Or give it any picture: Gemma lists what it sees, writes one line, and our rules check it.

On ten W3C videos we never tuned on, Gemma alone kept every not in {claim:e5.neg_gemma_k} of {claim:e5.neg_gemma_n} easy-read captions. AccessCast published {claim:e5.neg_ours_k} of {claim:e5.neg_ours_n}.
Against specialist translators, Gemma won on one of two scores in all five languages, and lost on the other for three. We report that.

Every Gemma call runs on AMD's Token Factory: {claim:amd.requests} requests and {claim:amd.tokens_millions} tokens, from our own logs. A finished minute of the five versions we measured costs about {claim:cost.usd_per_min} of Gemma, at list price.

The law already asks for this: in Europe since {claim:cited.law.eaa_apply_date}, in India since {claim:cited.law.india_mib_ott_date}, and for US public universities from {claim:cited.law.ada_title2_large_date}.
AccessCast. Every viewer, the same video.
